analysis.one_liner: Creates a Medicare-style plan covering every U.S. resident, funded by taxes on high incomes and tobacco, alcohol, and sugary drinks.
analysis.headline: Introduced on December 19, 2018 with 13 days left in the 115th Congress, the bill was referred to five committees and received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a government-run health insurance program covering every U.S. resident, starting with a public option sold alongside private plans in 2020–2021 and a full program called Medicare for America beginning in 2022. It would cover doctor and hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, vision, hearing, mental health, and long-term care, with premiums set at zero for households under twice the poverty line and capped at a share of income for everyone else. It would pay for itself by rolling back the 2017 tax cuts, adding a surtax on high incomes, raising Medicare payroll and investment-income taxes, and raising excise taxes on tobacco, alcohol, and sugary drinks. It was introduced in the final days of a Congress controlled by the other party and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident, with the largest gains for low-income households, who would owe no premium, deductible, or cost-sharing; people with disabilities, who would no longer wait 24 months for Medicare; and anyone currently priced out of dental, vision, hearing, or long-term care, all of which become covered benefits. Patients would also gain protections against surprise balance billing and insurance requirements for prior authorization.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a national health insurance program covering all U.S. residents, including hospital care, prescription drugs, and dental services, fully implemented in 2022.

Premiums would be zero for households below 200% of the poverty line, capped at 9.69% of income, with deductibles no more than $350 per person and out-of-pocket costs capped at $3,500 per person ($0 for low-income households).

Covers benefits beyond standard Medicare and most employer plans, including dental, hearing aids, long-term home- and community-based care, family planning including abortion, gender-confirming care, and acupuncture.

Requires the Secretary to negotiate prescription drug prices, falling back to prices paid by the VA or other wealthy countries if negotiation fails, and excludes a manufacturer's entire product line if it refuses to negotiate.
Prohibits prior authorization and step-therapy requirements, and bans providers from balance-billing patients above the program's rates.

Funds the program by sunsetting the 2017 tax law (Public Law 115-97), adding a surtax, expanding the Medicare payroll tax and net investment income tax, and raising excise taxes on tobacco, alcohol, and sugared drinks.
Creates a transitional public plan option for 2020–2021, prioritizing areas where only one insurer offers plans or where competition is lacking, such as rural areas.

analysis.who_pays: Higher-income households, through a new surtax, an expanded net investment income tax, higher Medicare payroll taxes, and the rollback of the 2017 tax cuts; consumers of tobacco, alcohol, and sugary drinks, through higher excise taxes; holders of health savings and flexible spending accounts, whose accounts would be terminated; and large employers that do not offer qualifying plans, which would owe 8% of annual payroll.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, employers, and taxed consumers

drawbacks.text: The tax package is broad: it repeals the 2017 tax cuts, raises Medicare payroll and investment-income taxes, and raises excise taxes on tobacco, alcohol, and sugared drinks, which raise prices for consumers of those products.
Health savings accounts and flexible spending arrangements would be terminated, ending a tax-advantaged saving channel many households use for medical costs.

It would become unlawful for private insurers to sell coverage duplicating the public plan, ending most private insurance markets; private plans could survive only as supplemental coverage or as 'Medicare Advantage for America' contracts from 2026.
The program is premium-financed rather than fully tax-funded, so middle- and higher-income households would still owe monthly premiums of up to 9.69% of income on top of the new taxes.

The transition is long and phased over a decade: Medicaid and CHIP enrollments move over in stages through 2026, and states must keep paying 'maintenance of effort' contributions into the new trust fund through 2032 and beyond, which is where implementation disputes most plausibly arise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give every resident a comprehensive plan with low, income-based cost-sharing — one of the largest single improvements in economic security Congress has considered. The cost is equally real: substantial tax increases concentrated on high earners plus new excise taxes that reach consumers, the end of HSAs and FSAs, and the near-elimination of private health insurance markets. The main honest objections are about financing scale and transition risk rather than the coverage itself; the phased Medicaid shift and long-term state payments leave a decade where funding formulas could be renegotiated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 19, 2018, referred to five House committees, and sat there with no hearing or markup until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill, with Representative Jan Schakowsky as its one cosponsor, on December 19, 2018.
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, and the Judiciary.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and large employers kept the existing insurance system unchanged, and the 2017 tax law's rate cuts remained in effect.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Democrats, and it was introduced at the end of a Congress in which Republicans controlled the House.

industries.note: The bill ends the individual-market exchanges, makes duplicate private coverage unlawful, and reduces the role of employer plans, removing most of the private market. Insurers would survive mainly as Medicare Advantage for America contractors from 2026, so their interest in blocking the bill runs directly against the coverage gains for ordinary people.

Drug prices would be government-negotiated, with fallback to VA or international prices and exclusion of a manufacturer's entire product line if it refuses to negotiate, plus a review board barring excessive prices and a moratorium on direct-to-consumer advertising. Today's consumers pay more for drugs than beneficiaries under this plan would.

Payment would be set at no less than 110% of Medicare rates with extra support for underserved areas, and uncompensated care would largely disappear, but balance billing is banned and site-neutral payment cuts outpatient hospital revenue.

Participation is mandatory for Medicare providers and private top-up billing ends, but payment is guaranteed without prior authorization or step therapy, and primary care and behavioral health rates rise at least 20%.

Employers could keep offering qualifying plans or instead contribute 8% of payroll to the program; for employers whose health costs exceed that share, the requirement lowers expenses, while employees gain the right to opt into the public plan.
A new surtax, an expanded net investment income tax, higher Medicare payroll taxes, and repeal of the 2017 tax cuts fall on this group to fund universal coverage.

industries.industry: Tobacco, alcohol, and sugary drink producers
industries.note: Excise taxes rise on cigarettes, small cigars, other tobacco products, alcohol, and sugared drinks; the cost reaches their customers through higher prices.
